Decomposing differences in life expectancy

Source: vignettes/decomposition.Rmd
decomposition.Rmd

A difference in life expectancy, between deprivation quintiles, between two years or between two forecasts, is the sum of differences in death rates at many ages and from many causes. A decomposition attributes it to those ages and causes, and, for populations made of subgroups, separates the effect of the subgroups’ mortality from the effect of their composition. In mortensor this is a post-processing step, mt_decompose(), that works on observed data, on forecast draws, and on both together. Forecasts are decomposed draw by draw, so every contribution has an interval.

Method Decomposes Reference
"arriaga" (default for life expectancy) life expectancy, by age (and cause) Arriaga (1984), symmetric form as in Riffe et al. (2024)
"horiuchi" any function of the rates Horiuchi, Wilmoth and Pletcher (2008)
"stepwise" any function of the rates Andreev, Shkolnikov and Begun (2002)
"kitagawa" crude death rate: rates and age structure Kitagawa (1955)
groups with composition = "radix" life expectancy of a population of subgroups: subgroup rates and composition Riffe, Tursun-zade and Trias Llimós (2024), “Arriaga meets Kitagawa”
groups with composition = "pooled" life expectancy of the pooled rates: subgroup rates and age-specific composition Horiuchi et al. (2008) 
library(mortensor)
library(data.table)
x <- mt_data(deaths = ons_data, population = ons_data, by = c("sex", "imd_decile"), age = "age_group",
             value = c(deaths = "all_causes", population = "population"))
x <- mt_as_exposure(x, type = "midyear")
x <- mt_group_levels(x, "imd_decile", function(d) paste0("Q", ceiling(as.numeric(d) / 2)), name = "quintile")

The data are the ONS deaths and populations of England by sex, 5-year age group and IMD quintile, 2001-2019 (ons_data; Source: Office for National Statistics licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0). Q1 is the most deprived quintile.

The deprivation gap by age

Each quintile compared with Q1 in 2019, with 200 Poisson draws of the deaths for the intervals:

gap <- mt_decompose(x, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", periods = 2019, n_draws = 200)
gap
#> <mt_decomposition> life expectancy at 0, method arriaga; 8 comparison(s), 200 draw(s)
#>    comparison    sex   from     to period from_value to_value difference
#>         <int> <char> <char> <char>  <num>      <num>    <num>      <num>
#> 1:          1 female     Q1     Q2   2019     79.825   82.501      2.676
#> 2:          2 female     Q1     Q3   2019     79.825   83.930      4.105
#> 3:          3 female     Q1     Q4   2019     79.825   85.020      5.195
#> 4:          4 female     Q1     Q5   2019     79.825   86.290      6.465
#> 5:          5   male     Q1     Q2   2019     75.429   78.596      3.167
#> 6:          6   male     Q1     Q3   2019     75.429   80.604      5.174
#> 7:          7   male     Q1     Q4   2019     75.429   81.818      6.389
#> 8:          8   male     Q1     Q5   2019     75.429   83.094      7.665
#>    difference_q0.025 difference_q0.5 difference_q0.975 sum_contributions
#>                <num>           <num>             <num>             <num>
#> 1:             2.515           2.682             2.826             2.676
#> 2:             3.969           4.109             4.249             4.105
#> 3:             5.027           5.198             5.335             5.195
#> 4:             6.318           6.466             6.615             6.465
#> 5:             3.001           3.166             3.332             3.167
#> 6:             5.013           5.168             5.312             5.174
#> 7:             6.223           6.384             6.564             6.389
#> 8:             7.521           7.659             7.831             7.665
#>    max_residual
#>           <num>
#> 1:      1.3e-14
#> 2:      1.7e-14
#> 3:      1.5e-14
#> 4:      1.6e-14
#> 5:      1.6e-14
#> 6:      1.5e-14
#> 7:      1.6e-14
#> 8:      1.4e-14

The totals list one comparison per row: the life expectancy of the reference (from_value) and of the level (to_value), their difference with its interval, and the sum of the age contributions, which equals the difference (max_residual is the largest discrepancy over draws). summary(gap, by = "age") gives the contributions; the plot shows them for the gap between Q5 and Q1 (comparisons 4 and 8):

mt_plot_decomposition(gap, by = "age", comparisons = c(4, 8))

s <- summary(gap, by = "age")[to == "Q5"]
s[, band := cut(as.numeric(sub("[-+].*", "", age)), c(-1, 39, 64, 84, Inf),
                labels = c("0-39", "40-64", "65-84", "85+"))]
dcast(s[, .(contribution = round(sum(mean), 2)), by = .(sex, band)], sex ~ band, value.var = "contribution")
#> Key: <sex>
#>       sex  0-39 40-64 65-84   85+
#>    <char> <num> <num> <num> <num>
#> 1: female  0.55  2.01  3.20  0.70
#> 2:   male  0.93  3.01  3.29  0.43

The gap of 6.5 years for women and 7.7 years for men comes mostly from ages 40 to 84 (5.2 and 6.3 years): deaths at working ages and in early old age are much more frequent in Q1. Ages below 40 add 0.6 years for women and 0.9 years for men; infant mortality alone adds 0.2 years for women. With Poisson draws of the observed deaths, the intervals of single ages are narrow.

The methods agree closely. Symmetric Arriaga and symmetric stepwise replacement are identical for life expectancy, because Arriaga’s decomposition is stepwise replacement from the oldest to the youngest age; the line integral assigns interactions between ages slightly differently:

meth <- rbindlist(lapply(c("arriaga", "horiuchi", "stepwise"), function(m) {
  d <- mt_decompose(x, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", periods = 2019, method = m)
  summary(d, by = "age")[to == "Q5" & sex == "female", .(age, method = m, mean = round(mean, 3))]
}))
meth[, age := factor(age, unique(age))]
dcast(meth, age ~ method, value.var = "mean")[age %in% c("0", "40-44", "60-64", "75-79", "90+")]
#> Key: <age>
#>       age arriaga horiuchi stepwise
#>    <fctr>   <num>    <num>    <num>
#> 1:      0   0.221    0.221    0.221
#> 2:  40-44   0.232    0.231    0.232
#> 3:  60-64   0.651    0.650    0.651
#> 4:  75-79   0.881    0.886    0.881
#> 5:    90+   0.276    0.272    0.276

Causes behind the gap

Causes of death are a stratum variable whose rates add up to all causes. cause names it, and the hierarchy tells mt_decompose() which level is the total. At ages 50 and over (as in “Causes of death by deprivation”):

causes <- names(ons_data)[-(1:7)]
xc <- mt_data(deaths = ons_data, population = ons_data, by = c("sex", "imd_decile", "cause"),
              age = "age_group", value = list(deaths = c(all = "all_causes", causes), population = "population"))
xc <- mt_as_exposure(xc, type = "midyear")
xc <- mt_subset(xc, ages = c(50, Inf), periods = c(2019, 2019))
xc <- mt_group_levels(xc, "imd_decile", function(d) paste0("Q", ceiling(as.numeric(d) / 2)), name = "quintile")
xc <- mt_group_levels(xc, "cause", ons_cause_groups, other = "rest", total = "all", additive = "rates")
gc <- mt_decompose(xc, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", cause = "cause",
                   hierarchy = mt_hierarchy(cause = "all", additive = "rates"))
sc <- summary(gc, by = "cause")[to == "Q5"]
dcast(sc, cause ~ sex, value.var = "mean")[order(-female), lapply(.SD, function(v) if (is.numeric(v)) round(v, 2) else v)]
#>                 cause female  male
#>                <char>  <num> <num>
#>  1:              rest   1.37  1.42
#>  2:       respiratory   0.89  0.77
#>  3:       lung_cancer   0.71  0.71
#>  4:               ihd   0.65  1.09
#>  5:     other_cancers   0.54  0.65
#>  6:          dementia   0.52  0.34
#>  7:     liver_alcohol   0.28  0.51
#>  8:            stroke   0.21  0.21
#>  9: other_circulatory   0.18  0.17
#> 10:          diabetes   0.12  0.12
#> 11: colorectal_cancer   0.04  0.09
#> 12:   breast_prostate   0.04  0.07
mt_plot_decomposition(gc, by = "age", fill = "cause", comparisons = c(4, 8))

Each age contribution is split over the causes in proportion to their rate differences (Riffe et al. 2024, eqs. 12-13). Of the gap in life expectancy at 50, respiratory diseases, lung cancer and ischaemic heart disease contribute most among the named causes, for both sexes, and the remaining causes together (rest) contribute a large share. Causes with higher rates in Q5 than in Q1 would have negative contributions.

Change over time and the composition of England

The life expectancy of England changes because the mortality of every quintile changes and because the population shifts between quintiles. Riffe, Tursun-zade and Trias Llimós (2024) treat the life expectancy of a population of subgroups as the mean of the subgroups’ life expectancies, weighted by their shares at the start of life (the radix). A Kitagawa decomposition of that mean separates the composition from the change within each subgroup, which is then split by age:

eng <- mt_decompose(x, periods = c(2001, 2019), groups = "quintile")
eng
#> <mt_decomposition> life expectancy at 0, method arriaga, radix composition; 2 comparison(s), 1 draw(s)
#>    comparison    sex   from     to from_value to_value difference
#>         <int> <char> <char> <char>      <num>    <num>      <num>
#> 1:          1 female   2001   2019     80.418   83.139      2.721
#> 2:          2   male   2001   2019     75.721   79.463      3.742
#>    sum_contributions max_residual
#>                <num>        <num>
#> 1:             2.721      3.1e-15
#> 2:             3.742      1.3e-15
summary(eng, by = c("component", "group"))[, .(sex, component, group, mean = round(mean, 3))]
#>        sex   component  group   mean
#>     <char>      <char> <char>  <num>
#>  1: female        rate     Q1  0.543
#>  2: female        rate     Q2  0.600
#>  3: female        rate     Q3  0.549
#>  4: female        rate     Q4  0.536
#>  5: female        rate     Q5  0.589
#>  6: female composition   <NA> -0.096
#>  7:   male        rate     Q1  0.947
#>  8:   male        rate     Q2  0.825
#>  9:   male        rate     Q3  0.737
#> 10:   male        rate     Q4  0.703
#> 11:   male        rate     Q5  0.658
#> 12:   male composition   <NA> -0.128

Life expectancy at birth of England, computed this way, rose by 2.7 years for women and 3.7 years for men. Every quintile contributed about half a year or more; for men, Q1 contributed most. The composition effect is negative: in 2019 a larger share of births was in the more deprived quintiles than in 2001. The deciles are defined by the IMD version of each year, so the shares partly reflect reclassification of areas.

The radix-weighted life expectancy is not the life expectancy of the pooled rates of England, which weight the quintiles by their population at each age (Vaupel 2002 calls these “current conditions” and “current rates”). composition = "pooled" decomposes the latter, with the shares at every age as parameters of a line-integral decomposition:

eng_pooled <- mt_decompose(x, periods = c(2001, 2019), groups = "quintile", composition = "pooled")
summary(eng_pooled, by = NULL)[, .(sex, from_value, to_value, difference)]
#>       sex from_value to_value difference
#>    <char>      <num>    <num>      <num>
#> 1: female   80.64917 83.63128   2.982103
#> 2:   male   76.02971 79.98056   3.950856
summary(eng_pooled, by = c("component", "group"))[, .(sex, component, group, mean = round(mean, 3))]
#>        sex   component  group  mean
#>     <char>      <char> <char> <num>
#>  1: female        rate     Q1 0.462
#>  2: female        rate     Q2 0.568
#>  3: female        rate     Q3 0.601
#>  4: female        rate     Q4 0.615
#>  5: female        rate     Q5 0.635
#>  6: female composition   <NA> 0.101
#>  7:   male        rate     Q1 0.854
#>  8:   male        rate     Q2 0.799
#>  9:   male        rate     Q3 0.785
#> 10:   male        rate     Q4 0.783
#> 11:   male        rate     Q5 0.696
#> 12:   male composition   <NA> 0.033
E <- mt_array(x, "exposure")
women <- x$strata$label[x$strata$sex == "female"]
round(rbind(birth_2001 = E["0", "2001", women], birth_2019 = E["0", "2019", women],
            age75_2001 = E["75-79", "2001", women], age75_2019 = E["75-79", "2019", women]) /
        rep(c(sum(E["0", "2001", women]), sum(E["0", "2019", women]), sum(E["75-79", "2001", women]),
              sum(E["75-79", "2019", women])), 5), 3)
#>            female.Q1 female.Q2 female.Q3 female.Q4 female.Q5
#> birth_2001     0.249     0.204     0.184     0.178     0.184
#> birth_2019     0.252     0.223     0.195     0.175     0.156
#> age75_2001     0.188     0.200     0.211     0.208     0.193
#> age75_2019     0.143     0.175     0.211     0.232     0.239

The pooled life expectancy is 0.2 to 0.5 years higher, and its composition effect is positive. The shares explain the difference: at birth the share of Q5 fell (from 18% to 16% for girls), while at ages 75-79, where many deaths occur, it rose from 19% to 24% and the share of Q1 fell from 19% to 14%. The two decompositions answer different questions; the radix version is the one of Riffe et al. and is exact, the pooled one matches the life expectancy published for the whole population. The composition effect is a single number (radix) or one per age (pooled): the separate composition terms of the subgroups are not identified.

Forecasts

Li-Lee forecasts to 2035, decomposed draw by draw. With draws, periods can combine an observed year (held in the draws) with forecast years:

fc <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(li_lee(common_by = "sex"), x), to = 2035, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
change <- mt_decompose(fc, periods = c(2019, 2035))
summary(change, by = NULL)[, .(sex, quintile, from_value, to_value, difference, difference_q0.025,
                               difference_q0.975)]
#>        sex quintile from_value to_value difference difference_q0.025
#>     <char>   <char>      <num>    <num>      <num>             <num>
#>  1: female       Q1   79.83321 83.38002   3.546810        -0.4746512
#>  2: female       Q2   82.49875 85.19000   2.691251        -0.9157246
#>  3: female       Q3   83.93153 86.29470   2.363171        -0.9994910
#>  4: female       Q4   85.01728 87.04342   2.026131        -1.1991626
#>  5: female       Q5   86.29508 87.95801   1.662930        -1.3416993
#>  6:   male       Q1   75.43067 79.56163   4.130958         1.9716285
#>  7:   male       Q2   78.59779 82.07083   3.473034         1.5525868
#>  8:   male       Q3   80.60501 83.66165   3.056633         1.3083920
#>  9:   male       Q4   81.82001 84.69466   2.874653         1.1883222
#> 10:   male       Q5   83.08997 85.79980   2.709830         1.1197734
#>     difference_q0.975
#>                 <num>
#>  1:          7.056338
#>  2:          5.833867
#>  3:          5.259254
#>  4:          4.759013
#>  5:          4.286227
#>  6:          6.373607
#>  7:          5.442919
#>  8:          4.848403
#>  9:          4.601860
#> 10:          4.325339
mt_plot_decomposition(change, by = "age", comparisons = c(1, 5))

The forecast gain of women in Q1 (3.5 years by 2035) comes mostly from ages 50 to 84 (2.5 years). The bars give the mean contribution and the lines the 95% interval of each age over the draws. The intervals are wide and include zero at most ages: the common trend of Li-Lee is uncertain 16 years ahead, and it moves all ages together, so the uncertainty of the ages adds up in the total (its interval is in the table above).

The gap between Q5 and Q1, observed in 2019 and forecast for 2035:

g <- mt_decompose(fc, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", periods = c(2019, 2035))
sg <- summary(g, by = "age")[to == "Q5" & sex == "female"]
sg[, age := factor(age, unique(age))]
dcast(sg, age ~ period, value.var = "mean")[, lapply(.SD, function(v) if (is.numeric(v)) round(v, 3) else v)]
#> Key: <age>
#>        age   2019  2035
#>     <fctr>  <num> <num>
#>  1:      0  0.221 0.147
#>  2:    1-4  0.036 0.017
#>  3:    5-9 -0.003 0.009
#>  4:  10-14  0.030 0.010
#>  5:  15-19  0.027 0.012
#>  6:  20-24  0.002 0.010
#>  7:  25-29  0.043 0.029
#>  8:  30-34  0.031 0.067
#>  9:  35-39  0.159 0.122
#> 10:  40-44  0.232 0.181
#> 11:  45-49  0.272 0.229
#> 12:  50-54  0.350 0.278
#> 13:  55-59  0.501 0.372
#> 14:  60-64  0.651 0.475
#> 15:  65-69  0.766 0.532
#> 16:  70-74  0.843 0.568
#> 17:  75-79  0.881 0.565
#> 18:  80-84  0.716 0.492
#> 19:  85-89  0.428 0.304
#> 20:    90+  0.276 0.158
#>        age   2019  2035
#>     <fctr>  <num> <num>

Li-Lee narrows the female gap from 6.5 to 4.6 years mainly at ages 60 to 84, where its deviations of Q1 from the common trend return towards their average (see “Forecasting mortality by deprivation quintile”).

Two forecasts of the same year are compared by giving the second as y. Lee-Carter per quintile against Li-Lee, for 2035:

fl <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(lee_carter(), x), to = 2035, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
mm <- mt_decompose(fc, fl, periods = 2035)
summary(mm, by = NULL)[sex == "female", .(quintile, from_value, to_value, difference)]
#>    quintile from_value to_value difference
#>      <char>      <num>    <num>      <num>
#> 1:       Q1   83.38002 81.45818 -1.9218316
#> 2:       Q2   85.19000 84.66799 -0.5220072
#> 3:       Q3   86.29470 86.20373 -0.0909772
#> 4:       Q4   87.04342 87.46871  0.4252962
#> 5:       Q5   87.95801 89.20283  1.2448255
mt_plot_decomposition(mm, by = "age", comparisons = c(1, 5))

For women in Q1, Lee-Carter forecasts 1.9 years less than Li-Lee, 1.5 years of it at ages 60 and over: Lee-Carter extrapolates the slower improvement of Q1 at these ages in 2001-2019, while Li-Lee lets Q1 return towards the common trend of all quintiles.

Other quantities

quantity selects the summary. The probability of dying between 30 and 75 and the age-standardised rate are decomposed by age with the line integral; any function of the rates can be given as well:

pd <- mt_decompose(x, periods = c(2001, 2019), quantity = "prob_dying", at = 30, to = 75)
summary(pd, by = NULL)[sex == "male", .(quintile, from_value, to_value, difference)]
#>    quintile from_value  to_value  difference
#>      <char>      <num>     <num>       <num>
#> 1:       Q1  0.4928583 0.3893294 -0.10352894
#> 2:       Q2  0.4081154 0.2966236 -0.11149177
#> 3:       Q3  0.3401629 0.2389755 -0.10118739
#> 4:       Q4  0.3045689 0.2098098 -0.09475918
#> 5:       Q5  0.2653566 0.1775151 -0.08784144

The crude death rate changes with the rates and with the age structure of the population. Kitagawa’s decomposition separates the two:

cr <- mt_decompose(x, periods = c(2001, 2019), quantity = "crude_rate")
dcast(summary(cr, by = "component"), sex + quintile ~ component, value.var = "mean")[
  , lapply(.SD, function(v) if (is.numeric(v)) round(v) else v)]
#> Key: <sex, quintile>
#>        sex quintile composition  rate
#>     <char>   <char>       <num> <num>
#>  1: female       Q1         -56  -138
#>  2: female       Q2         -23  -214
#>  3: female       Q3          69  -270
#>  4: female       Q4         155  -279
#>  5: female       Q5         262  -301
#>  6:   male       Q1          97  -287
#>  7:   male       Q2         141  -314
#>  8:   male       Q3         240  -350
#>  9:   male       Q4         319  -357
#> 10:   male       Q5         399  -340

Per 100,000, falling rates lowered the crude death rate of every quintile by 140 to 360 deaths. Ageing raised it, most in the least deprived quintiles, whose populations are oldest; only for women in Q1 and Q2 did the age structure lower it. For men in Q5 the crude rate rose although the rates fell.

Choosing a method

  • Life expectancy by age and cause: "arriaga" (exact and fast). Other quantities: "horiuchi" or "stepwise"; the line integral distributes interactions evenly, stepwise replacement depends on the order of the ages.
  • Populations of subgroups: composition = "radix" for the decomposition of Riffe et al.; "pooled" when the target is the life expectancy of the whole population as usually published.
  • Forecasts: contributions and their sums come with intervals, because every draw is decomposed. Sums over ages or causes are formed draw by draw (summary(by = )), so their intervals are not sums of intervals.
  • Cause-specific contributions are only as good as the coding of causes; trends in coding (dementia, ill-defined causes) move between causes, not in the total.

References

Andreev EM, Shkolnikov VM, Begun AZ (2002). Algorithm for decomposition of differences between aggregate demographic measures and its application to life expectancies, healthy life expectancies, parity-progression ratios and total fertility rates. Demographic Research 7: 499-522.

Arriaga EE (1984). Measuring and explaining the change in life expectancies. Demography 21(1): 83-96.

Horiuchi S, Wilmoth JR, Pletcher SD (2008). A decomposition method based on a model of continuous change. Demography 45(4): 785-801.

Kitagawa EM (1955). Components of a difference between two rates. Journal of the American Statistical Association 50(272): 1168-1194.

Riffe T, Tursun-zade R, Trias Llimós S (2024). Arriaga meets Kitagawa. Life expectancy decomposition with population subgroups. MPIDR Working Paper WP-2024-029. doi:10.4054/MPIDR-WP-2024-029.

Vaupel JW (2002). Life expectancy at current rates vs. current conditions: a reflexion stimulated by Bongaarts and Feeney’s “How long do we live?”. Demographic Research 7: 365-378.
